name: Computer Vision

claims.claim_text: A camera-based alternative to analytic kinematics is to command a motion, observe with a camera where the arm actually ended up, and let the mapping from command to observed position build up empirically.
claims.quote_verbatim: And what you do is you point a camera at the damn thing and then you move it and then you say, all right, I moved this thing. Now, where is it?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Back Into The Swing Of Things

claims.claim_text: Early BeagleBoard vision projects paired the board with a Kinect through the LibFreenect driver to build 3D maps and run face recognition on flying platforms.
claims.quote_verbatim: And people put connects on these things. And they run LibFreenect. And they can take in all that data from their connect. And they'll build 3D maps and recognize people's faces.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: National Instruments shipped camera drivers with packaged object-recognition vision software, so machine-builders could avoid spending months writing their own recognition code.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can hook up a camera to the National Instruments driver and they've got like vision software which can do object recognition and all that sort of stuff. It's already done for you.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Industrial machine-safety systems were built as DSP-based embedded computer vision, with camera feedback as the sensing front end, well before general-purpose embedded CPUs could handle the load.
claims.quote_verbatim: they basically wanted somebody to come down and basically work on a DSP system, an embedded computer vision system effectively
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: A practical way to give a machine vision-based registration on raw stock is to apply printed fiducial stickers to the workpiece for the camera to locate.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's a computer vision. They have the stickers that go on the wood.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Fixed-function video codec blocks are the right silicon answer for a settled standard like H.264 because no programmable engine will beat a dedicated IP block or ASIC on speed; imaging and vision algorithms are the opposite case, unstandardized and still changing.
claims.quote_verbatim: Versus, let's say, an H.264 is a solved problem, right? People banging into a little IP block or an ASIC. And it's not going to be faster than that.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Programmability in a video pipeline earns its keep mainly when you must support multiple standards or a standard still in flux, which is a secondary concern compared with raw throughput.
claims.quote_verbatim: Now, sometimes there's an advantage to have programmability. Because you can do multi-standards. And if the standard is involving.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: A vision workload is not just frame capture: it decomposes into filtering, object detection, and semantic interpretation of the detected objects, each stage adding compute on top of the last.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to filter, you have to detect objects. You have to make sense of the objects. It's a very, very tough problem.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Vision workloads are the dividing line where dropping a Linux-class board into a design beats hand-optimizing a tiny microcontroller, because a 4K-flash part cannot hold the software stack at any reasonable engineering cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're doing vision and all that sort of stuff, you're not going to go, well, I'm going to choose my pick with 4k of memory and I'm going to hand code this thing in assembler.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: Choosing a minimal processor and hand-writing assembly for a vision-equipped robot purely as an engineering challenge is poor engineering when a capable application processor is available.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're going back and writing everything yourself in assembler on, you know, some tiny little crazy small processor, just because you can, and it's an engineering challenge, you're doing it wrong.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: Low-cost FPGA boards made it plausible to put high-end vision on a drone for roughly fifty dollars, which was the kind of problem that would stymie a non-FPGA solution.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put vision, you know, like some high-end vision on a drone for, you know, 50 bucks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: An FPGA sitting directly behind the image sensor can do real-time feature extraction and motion detection and hand only the results to a downstream processing board, turning the camera into a smart peripheral.
claims.quote_verbatim: And we're working on that same thing as well. We've got an FPGA-based camera in the works that'll be a peripheral device to a processing board as well.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Hardware test robots can be driven by running OpenCV over a video feed or camera pointed at the device screen, locating a UI element visually and then physically tapping it.
claims.quote_verbatim: where I use the open CV library, I'm using either a video feed off the device or a camera. And then I'm using, uh, open computer vision magic to find elements on the screen, converting that to an element and then clicking that.
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: A structured vision course collapsed the unknowns on a self-directed robotics vision project from roughly 95 percent to 40 percent, largely by teaching enough Python and OpenCV that the remaining gaps became searchable.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would have 95% unknowns, but because of the class, I, I learned Python much better. I learned open computer, open CV much better.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: LIDAR is compelling for one-time high-detail street mapping, where a single drive produces a detailed 3D model, but that does not make it the necessary sensing technology for the driving task itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: lighter is very interesting for, for stuff like mapping where you have a car driving down the street once, and then you have like a very detailed 3d model of everything in that street. Um, but for actual self-driving cars, I'm, I'm not, I'm not convinced yet that lighter will actually be the technology for that.
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: A recurring smart-camera module concept is a camera plus FPGA or fast microcontroller running OpenCV, pre-programmed for generic tasks and exposing a simple output such as a motion-detected flag rather than a video stream.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was going to do one of these, like a little module that had cameras and FPGA and, or whatever, some super whiz bang micro that was running open, uh, open CV
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: Connectomics imaging cuts a tissue sample into about 26,000 ultrathin sections carried on electron-transparent tape through an automated microscope, with roughly six months of continuous imaging to capture the full stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: cut it into 26,000 thin sections, load each one of those thin sections onto a reel of electron transparent tape, load that tape into a modified microscope that can automatically run this tape. Spend six months imaging that whole thing.
claims.speaker: Adam McCombs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam McCombs

claims.claim_text: Electron-microscope imaging of tissue requires staining with a heavy metal, osmium tetroxide, purely to create enough image contrast, which necessarily kills the sample.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to, uh, uh, kind of get a heavy metal into the sample to get enough contrast on the image. And use what's called osmine tetroxide for that.
claims.speaker: Adam McCombs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam McCombs

claims.claim_text: The sample is microwaved during staining so cells die without changing shape, preserving the geometric connectivity that the downstream 3D reconstruction depends on.
claims.quote_verbatim: you actually have to microwave the sample while you're staining it. So you've very thoroughly killed every cell in this thing. You just done it very carefully. So the cells don't change shape when they're killed.
claims.speaker: Adam McCombs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam McCombs

claims.claim_text: Vision is adequate to close the loop in robotics because the goal is only to land inside a tolerance envelope, whereas CNC machining demands precise control of every axis at every instant and cannot be served the same way.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're trying to get to a target, but you might not really care, you know, as long as it stays within an envelope that it gets there. So you could use vision, you know, to close the loop. But, uh, with CNC, you, you really have to precisely control every little aspect of it.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Robotic welding is hard because the job is defined by imperfect fit-up: a human welder's skill is producing a sound weld from parts that do not meet as drawn.
claims.quote_verbatim: Welders take a look at imperfect conditions and make a perfect weld. That's their job.
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The investment case for robotic welding opened when three things converged: better computer vision, LIDAR-derived point clouds for geometry, and arms that were already cheap and getting cheaper.
claims.quote_verbatim: we started to look at advances in, again, computer vision, point cloud generation via LIDAR and then the fact that arms and stuff were already relatively inexpensive and getting less expensive
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Replacing physical protection such as armour and bumpers with camera-based obstacle avoidance trades bill-of-materials and mechanical work for software effort that someone still has to write.
claims.quote_verbatim: You just have a camera and just do it all visually and throw. I guess. I mean, he's got to write the code for that then, though.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Knob and Tube Wiring

claims.claim_text: Livestock health monitoring works by recording pens continuously and recognizing anatomical features such as ears, tails and legs, then classifying animals as healthy or abnormal from those features.
claims.quote_verbatim: has cameras recording pig pens, right? And he's recognizing all the features, you know, the ears and the tails and the legs and everything like that.
claims.episode_title: Embedded Linux with Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: A spatial-AI camera module can output object identity plus XYZ coordinates in meters as metadata, so a downstream motor controller receives coordinates rather than pixels.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do things like, you know, perceive a water bottle and get its XYZ coordinates in meters, and then just get that as metadata out to some, you know, motor controller, driver, microcontroller
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Because the vision result is a few bytes rather than a video stream, the perception module can hang off an 8-bit ATmega or an ESP32 over SPI instead of requiring a host computer.
claims.quote_verbatim: So not like a whole computer, but it's true embedded. So you can have like an SPI output to, you know, an AT-Mega if you want, or to an ESP32.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Rear-approach collisions are the case for automated bike sensing because the rider is aware of the impending impact only about 20 percent of the time.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it turns out that only like 20% of the time, do you, as the person riding the bike, know you're about to get run over because you're getting run over from behind.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Spatial perception differs from image classification in that the output is an object's distance and trajectory in the physical world, not merely a label saying the object is present in the frame.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's not just image classification. Like, Oh, there's a dog in that image, but it's like, there's a dog 30 feet in that direction going this trajectory sort of thing.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Classical CV and neural inference do different jobs on the same device: the network supplies identity, while CV routines supply real-time lossless digital zoom and feature tracking.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then like CV, which is like, allows you to do like, you know, real time, uh, real time digital zoom, like lossless zoom and feature tracking, all these other complicated CV functions.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: OpenCV's DNN module runs inference for models trained in PyTorch or TensorFlow, and pairing it with OpenVINO yielded roughly tenfold speedups across a range of platforms.
claims.quote_verbatim: whether you're doing PyTorch or TensorFlow, they have their DNN module, which allows you to, to execute these models more performantly. And it pairs with OpenVINO. So you can get like 10X increases across a variety of platforms.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Before on-device inference, deploying vision meant streaming video to a cloud service or to a human watching, which made many applications economically intractable.
claims.quote_verbatim: computer vision was just totally intractable before because computer vision meant you had to stream to AWS or you had to stream the video for someone to look at it
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Encoding a vision result as a single state byte with CRC room, using a byte's 255 values to cover roughly 20 states of interest, lets a fleet of cameras report over a low-bandwidth LoRa link at kilobytes per second.
claims.quote_verbatim: because maybe there's like 20 states you want to look at and you have 255 possible in a byte
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: In commercial fishing the vision algorithms for counting fish and identifying species were already adequate; the blocker to deployment was never the models.
claims.quote_verbatim: the computer vision algorithms are actually already capable of doing what they need. Counting the number of fish, detecting the species of fish, all the AI models can already do this
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Underwater fishing cameras sit around two kilometers from the vessel and RF is absorbed within about two feet of water, so wireless video backhaul is not an option.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're wanting the cameras to be two kilometers away from you typically.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Neither cable choice works for long subsea camera runs: copper corrodes, and fiber resists corrosion but cannot be repaired in the field, on top of consuming vessel space needed for catch.
claims.quote_verbatim: So copper cable corroding, you're getting cramped. You do fiber optic. Great. Then it doesn't corrode, but you can't feel to repair it.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: On-device processing gives roughly a billion-to-one compression, turning incoming 10 gigabit per second video into an output of fish counts, sizes and species.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have this like billion to one compression effectively on device, where it's this high bandwidth, 10 gigabit per second video feeds that are coming in. And then your output is just counts of fish
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Once the payload is small enough, results can be carried acoustically through water, which propagates kilometers easily and leaves room for many frequency-division-multiplexed channels in the audio spectrum.
claims.quote_verbatim: the data actually sent back over just sound waves in the water, like dolphin stock. Right. And that goes kilometers really easily.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: A common collision-avoidance false positive is a parked car directly ahead that the driver intends to steer around: the system reads the closing trajectory as an imminent crash because it has no model of the planned maneuver.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're basically are actually heading straight to another car, but it's actually a parked car that you're going to steer around, you know, when you get to it, but it doesn't know that yet. It thinks you're going to crash into it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A camera-only driver assistance system was fooled by a large printed advertisement of a face on the back of a bus, reading the image as a pedestrian stepping out.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was this Tesla that, that famously was fooled by a big advertisement of somebody's face on the back of the bus
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Camera-only perception degrades in exactly the conditions where driving is hardest, at night and in rain, because there is no complementary ranging sensor to fall back on.
claims.quote_verbatim: especially at night and in the rain and all sorts of, you know, crap because the, the Tesla only has cameras. It doesn't have, you know, LIDAR and stuff
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: One argument for camera-only autonomy is existence proof: human drivers operate with two eyes and no ranging sensor, making LIDAR a stopgap for the period when the optics and processing are not yet good enough.
claims.quote_verbatim: What are the sensing things on a normal manual driven car? Two eyeballs. You, you don't have like LIDAR. So it clearly can be done with a, with optically. And LIDAR is almost like a stop gap for when you can't make the optics work as well as they could do.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A schematic symbol builder can be constructed from classical techniques alone: OCR plus simple line and table detection on a highlighted region of a datasheet pin table, with no learned model required.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses OCR, optical character recognition and computer vision, simple computer vision to detect the table and lines. And what it does is it extracts the information from the table.
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Beyond extracting the pin table text, the tool infers electrical type per pin, classifying each as input, output or power so the generated symbol is usable.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can detect, is this an input? Is it an output? Is it a power pin? And we try our best to detect what it is and categorize the pin appropriately
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Computer vision and intelligent sensing became the beachhead market for a new FPGA family, specifically industrial and other cameras that fuse multiple sensing modes onto one platform.
claims.quote_verbatim: we are try on currently is super successful in surrounding computer visions and also intelligent sensing so we are doing very well in industrial cameras all types of visual cameras
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: Smaller vision customers were shut out of FPGAs not by capability but by price, cost and power, which their products could not absorb.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of my smaller customers had a tough time working with FPGA because they need to innovate with FPGA but the price cost power would never allow them to survive
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: Battery-powered outdoor vision such as a trail camera works by duty cycling, waking to capture a frame and returning to sleep, and typically needs a separate co-processor for the detection step.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you had a trail camera, you wanted to detect things, you wake up, take a photo, go back to sleep. That sort of thing. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Usually you need some kind of co-processing.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Here for a reason

claims.claim_text: A robot's mechanical characteristics drift over its service life as microcracks develop, so embedded sensors and actively compensating algorithms are needed rather than a fixed calibration.
claims.quote_verbatim: the characteristics of the robot change with time as it like, you know, wears and tears because, you know, micro cracks develop all over the place and like, you know, the system overall changes. So you need like embedded sensors and you need essentially like active algorithms that are compensating for whatever is happening with the gripper.
claims.speaker: Amitabh Shrivastava
claims.episode_title: Refrigerators and Robots with Amitabh Shrivastava

claims.claim_text: In warehouse picking, grasp success is usually verified with a camera rather than with force or tactile sensing in the gripper.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just solve it with vision, especially in like, you know, a kind of warehousing kind of thing, you know, if it has caught something or not
claims.speaker: Amitabh Shrivastava
claims.episode_title: Refrigerators and Robots with Amitabh Shrivastava

claims.claim_text: A packaged person sensor combines a camera and processor in one part and exposes only an I2C output reporting whether a person is in frame, which is all many designs actually need.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they sell this thing called the person sensor. And it's a camera. And it's a chip on the back. And it's got I squared C output. And it just spits out whether there's a person in the frame or not.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Engineering Optimization

claims.claim_text: NVIDIA's Jetson TK1, released around 2015, was the platform that made robot-mounted computer vision practical for hobbyists, and successor Tegra parts ended up inside AR headsets such as Magic Leap.
claims.quote_verbatim: NVIDIA released their Jetson TK1 developer board. So I got one of those and was playing with tons of computer vision stuff on it because, you know, it was a great platform, you know, that you could put on a robot.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: SLAM, simultaneous localization and mapping, tracks the pose of one or more cameras, often fused with IMUs, while simultaneously building a map of the surroundings.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's simultaneous localization and mapping, which is this sort of computer vision topic of taking one camera, multiple cameras, perhaps other sensors like IMUs, you know, and tracking the location of this camera unit in space
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: SLAM is only required if rendered graphics must stay anchored to real-world surfaces; a head-locked display that moves with the user's field of view needs none of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: In a lot of cases, you know, that may not even be necessary if you don't need to have objects anchored to the real world.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: On an all-day wearable, power consumption rather than algorithm availability is the binding constraint on cameras and SLAM, so each vision feature must justify its energy budget against its usability gain.
claims.quote_verbatim: the challenge with slam and cameras in general with my designs is just power consumption, because you don't want to spend too much power on processing for these sorts of computer vision tasks
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller-class system cannot realistically run full SLAM, but simple optical flow for tracking user translation is within reach on the same hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: the processing on board this device, you know, is a microcontroller style system. It's not necessarily the best thing in the world for doing something complex like slam
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: With a single-camera power budget the design choice is inward or outward: an inward camera gives blink detection and gaze input, an outward camera gives world tracking, and you cannot afford both.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could point it at the user's eye, you know, and detect blinks, potentially, you know, track the direction that they're looking for input. Or you could point it at the world.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: An SoC pairing a DSP with a Cortex-M33 lets vision processing be offloaded to the DSP rather than burning the application core on pixel work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the SOC I use has a has a DSP as well as a Cortex M33. So you could program the DSP to, you know, offload some of that vision stuff.
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Application processors that pair a main core with a low-power secondary processor are aimed at always-watching vision products such as smart doorbells.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think what they're going for here is this is like a targeting vision application. So like a smart doorbell or something like that.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Simulating doors falling off

claims.claim_text: A gesture-recognition demo ran on a plain Arduino board with local inference using a black-and-white camera, which is enough resolution and color depth to classify hand shapes.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it was using that camera. And because it's like black and white, it can look at your hand.
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel
claims.episode_title: Changing Course with Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Object detection was historically too computationally intensive for anything but powerful CPUs or GPUs; what changed is the combination of faster hardware and optimized software that brought it to embedded devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the new thing is getting powerful enough hardware and optimized enough software that we can now do things like object detection, which has traditionally been very computationally intensive
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel
claims.episode_title: Changing Course with Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: The frame-rate gap is stark: a laptop handles object detection at 60 frames per second while a Raspberry Pi 4 a few years earlier managed roughly one frame per second, which is too slow to be useful.
claims.quote_verbatim: your laptop can, you know, 60 frames a second, no problem. Raspberry Pi, you know, three, four years ago on like the Pi 4, that was going to do it in like one frame a second.
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel
claims.episode_title: Changing Course with Shawn Hymel
